utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you Your Honour. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon to you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings -- can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour, gentlemen. Yes, I can fully understand the proceedings in my mother tongue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, and good afternoon to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. Also good afternoon to the Defence team. I am here together with Miss Patricia Sellers, my co-counsel, and Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink, our case manager, and today as acting case manager also Ms. Sanja Bokulic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones we represent the Defence of Mr. Naser Oric and with us are our legal assistant, Miss Jasmina Cosic and Miss Adisa Mehic, as well as our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good afternoon to you and your team. Any preliminaries? Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. For the scheduling, yesterday I contacted lead counsel, Madam Vidovic, with a view to the coming two witnesses. We have four trial days and of course no counsel can give any guarantee but we aim for, we try to handle each witness for one day, meaning four trial days and two days per witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I can assure you, Mr. Wubben, having read his prior statement here, that if you handed this witness to me, I would finish him in half an hour. I can assure you. So I thank you, of course, for undertaking to finish the two witnesses in four days, but to be honest with you, I don't think that is really a big deal. Yes, any comments or remarks or preliminaries from your side?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. No questions, but when it comes to the witness that the Prosecution is presenting today, it is an insider with very important knowledge, essential for our defence and that is why I consider that we shall need five or six hours for the cross-examination of that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It depends. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: In addition, you never know, Your Honour, what it might end up. But anyhow we have also another submission to do. I will leave that up to Ms. Patricia Sellers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, all right. I am going to make it very clear that I will only allow questions today, with this witness and the others that will follow, that are relevant to the case. I am not going to allow any more sittings in which you try to open up the whole history of the events that took place in Bosnia during the time. I mean, we have only got this accused here, a very limited number of events, and I am going to stick to those. Yes, is there a further point, issue, preliminary issue you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is one other preliminary issue. As to what you've just mentioned, we will certainly try our best to finish this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am pretty sure you will.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- with all due haste. The Prosecution would like to hand up to the Trial Chamber and to Defence today, these are pictures that should accompany Dr. Stankovic's expert report. The reason we're handing them up in compliance, actually, with the acceptance of his report into evidence is that these are -- these are coloured photos and the reason that you have black and white photos is that once we turn his expert report over to the Registry, the Registry photocopies things and therefore anything that was in colour becomes black and white. So what we wanted to do was to hand these up as, as a matter of fact they would be part of his expert report, but they're actually a replication of the photos that you already have, they're just in colour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any objection on your part?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. The other thing we wanted to tell you is this: That we will need to make some adjustments to today's timetable, or schedule, in that we need to finish, because of a prior commitment of one of the judges, we need to finish at 6.15, 6.30 at the latest. 6.15, I mean to be on the safe side. So I would suggest that we start, that we will have the shortest possible break and that there will not be a second break. We will continue until we finish. Of course, we will need to agree on how to do this with the technical staff and the interpreters. But let's start. Could you bring -- the witness does not have any protective measures in place that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to Mr. Bogilovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we proceed I want to make sure that what I will be saying and what will be said here in this courtroom in the English language is being translated to you into your own language. For the time being, are you receiving interpretation of what I am saying in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If at any time there are problems with interpretation, please draw our attention straight away, because it is important that you be able to follow every single word that is said here. Okay. You are here to give evidence in this case which the Prosecution has instituted against Naser Oric. I am the presiding Judge. My name is Carmel Agius and I come from the island of Malta. My right, I have Judge Hans Henrik Brydensholt, who comes from Denmark, the Kingdom of Denmark; and to my left I have Judge Albin Eser, who comes from Germany. Before you start giving evidence, our Rules require that you enter a solemn declaration. That's something similar and ultimately equivalent also to an oath. A solemn declaration that, in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this solemn declaration is going to be handed to you now by Mr. Usher. Please read it out loud and that will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a chair. You are going to be asked a series of questions first by Ms. Sellers, whom I suppose you have met already. She will then be followed by Madam Vidovic, who is appearing for Naser Oric. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bogilovic.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please state your name, your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Becir Bogilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, due to commentary at the start of the session I think I will try to lead the witness on areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead. The initial part I don't think are any problems there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, is it correct that you were born in Rogatica in Bosnia in 1950?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: It is correct that I was born on the 7th of January, 1950 in the Godomilje village, Rogatica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is it also correct your ethnic background is that of Bosnian Muslim?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, from December 1971 until June 1972, didn't you attend the police academy in Makarska, Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did. It was a course, a police course. For the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Pardon me. After you finished, you completed your police courses, did you receive employment as a police officer in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and before the course I spent three months working. After I completed my course, I continued to work and worked for 20 years, until September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And is that your testimony, that you worked for 20 years as a police officer in the Srebrenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: During your 20 years in the police force, did you take statements from victims, witnesses, or suspects in the normal course of your police work?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did all that. Everything provided for by the rules of service in the public security system.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you also, in the normal course of your police work, assist police inspectors in submitting criminal complaints to the court system?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers, although you and I are familiar with the term "police inspectors," I don't know if the same term has the same connotation in Yugoslavia. So I honestly don't know how this is being interpreted. I would suggest "his superiors" rather than "police inspectors."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bogilovic, were police inspectors superior to you within the chain of command of the police force?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were senior and we were subordinated to the komandirs or commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, did you also arrest persons and place them in detention in the normal course of your police work?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We arrested persons on the basis of written orders and oral orders, as well by a senior official or the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, as a police officer were you permitted or authorised to mistreat detained persons in your custody?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Of course not. We had to adhere to the rules of service governing the public security service.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Any police officer who mistreated a detainee, was he to be reported to a superior for disciplinary actions?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Disciplinary measures would be taken once the senior official was informed that anything like that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And what type of disciplinary measures would be taken in the event that a police officer had mistreated or harmed a detained person?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: That depended on the offence. If it was a lighter offence, then a fine would have to be made. If it was a more serious offence, or rather, a crime, then it would be handed over to the law courts and a criminal complaint would be filed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was the last post that you held on the police force in Srebrenica municipality that of a sector leader?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And as a sector leader, did you have responsibilities that extended into locations other than the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't like to -- I was sector leader for the sector that I provided security for.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did that include locations such as Podravanja, Suceska and that of Radosevici? Please pardon my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: They are local communes, six in all, where I was the sector leader.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, when you started working in Srebrenica, did your wife also move to Srebrenica with you and did you establish a family in Srebrenica during that 20-year time period?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. My wife came in 1972. The problem was with our accommodation. We had to rent a flat privately and received an apartment only later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, now I would like to turn your attention to March, April and May, 1992. Did there exist tensions at that time period between Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Serbs that affected the work of police stations or the work of political institutions in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the March, April and May 1992. At that time, I would say that it was almost a situation of war already. Of conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Were residents in Srebrenica, both Muslim and Serbs, fearful that there would be an outbreak of war at that time?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: They were afraid before that, because on the 17th of April it was decided to destroy a whole nation. An ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And as a result of what you have testified about, this decision, they, having decided to destroy a whole nation, did residents, both Muslim and Serbs, of Srebrenica leave the city?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. Everybody left the town of Srebrenica. 99 percent left the town of Srebrenica, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Sellers, because I think one of his statements needs to -- some clarification. You were asked, sir, whether the residents in Srebrenica, both the Muslims and the Serbs -- and I suppose also the Croats -- were fearful that there would be an outbreak of war at the time. And you said: They were afraid before that, because on the -- I heard you say 7th, but 17th of April we have here, it was decided to destroy a whole nation. And then you added, according to the transcript here, an ethnic group. What are you referring --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter notes that the interpreters added "ethnic group" as being nation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It began before that because when there was an attack on Bjeljina, Zvornik, the people saw that, watched that and they became afraid, and all that was before the 17th of April. The last talks with the Serbs were on the 17th of April and then there was an extended period until the 10th of April when Alija Hasic negotiated with them, and then Jokic Miodrag said, "There can be no more negotiations, everything is ours."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you are actually telling us that on the 17th of April, a decision was taken to, to cease all negotiations. Who took that decision? Miodrag Jokic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Miodrag Jokic. On that day, they -- the Arkan's men entered, as they were called, and I was in Bratunac at that time. They entered the area, occupied everything, put their men on duty and then Alija Hasic went to the Fontana Hotel in Bratunac once again and Miodrag said that to them, "There can be no more negotiations, everything is finished."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And who was Miodrag Jokic? It is not that I don't know, but I am not the only one hearing this case. Who was Miodrag Jokic? Whom did he represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Miodrag represented the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Was he in the government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think he was. Goran was the president, and he was in the government too, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, yes. I think that cleared the scenario for us. Yes, Ms. Sellers, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So Mr. Bogilovic, as a result of the events that took place on the 17th of April, did both Bosnian Muslims and Serbs start to leave the town, resulting in a diminishing of the population of about 99 percent, according to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. 80% had already left the town and the rest left on the 17th. The others left on the 17th and early in the morning of the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you also take your family away from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did take my family away on the 10th of April, 1992, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Where did you take your family to?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: At my wife's request and my children's and neighbour's request -- well, when I got home, they were all crying. I asked them what had happened. My daughter was 17 and a half, my wife was crying and screaming; she said, "I can't stay here, I don't want anybody to rape my child." The neighbours started to leave, and I said that -- said they would go with them. So I said would take them away and I would come back. And the neighbours had some friends in Herceg Novi. We arrived in Herceg Novi that evening, spent the night there, in the morning I went back to Titograd with them and handed over my wife and children with my sister-in-law in Titograd. That night I spent in Titograd, and that was the 11th, in the evening, and that evening we saw the Visegrad affair -- the Visegrad affair took place, the dam affair, and that was on the news, the affair of the dam at Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is the relevance of this, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would claim that the relevance is just showing that Srebrenica was -- dropped in population, including this witness's family left and that he took his family for fear of the outbreak. That was the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's leave it at that. Is this contested by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, this is background material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's move.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Bogilovic, did you then return to the municipality of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: I did return. On the 12th. By train from Bar to Belgrade and Titograd, Titovo Uzice. In Titovo Uzice, I got off and I went to the bus station. I saw the schedule, but there was no bus there. I waited for an hour, there was still no bus, so I asked at the information desk, asked them what as going on. They laughed and said, well, there's no bus. It's wartime. So I found this a little strange. And then the -- there was a bus from Titovo Uzice to Bajina Basta. I got in that bus and was taken to Bajina Basta. From Bajina Basta I went on on foot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop. The question that was put to you was a very simple one. Madam Sellers asked you: All right, Mr. Bogilovic, did you then return to the municipality of Srebrenica? All you needed to tell us --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- yes, I did return, and it was on the 12th of April. We don't need all of the rest of the information, because otherwise you will be here the next -- the whole of next week, believe me. If you keep giving us all of this information, you will be here for a week and a half. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did go back on the 12th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, between the time of mid-April until about mid-May, 1992, did you yourself witness and experience a build-up of violence between Muslims and Serbs? And please keep your answer limited and contained.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th, with the entry into Bosnia-Herzegovina from Serbia, I was stopped by the Serb police and they said that it was the Serb municipality of Skelani. I asked the man when that happened and he said it happened on the 10th of April. That's when the Skelani municipality was established, separate from the Srebrenica municipality. Two days later, they killed two Muslims, those same -- well the same municipality between Skelani and Jezero.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, could I ask you then, during the time period between April and May 1992, would it be your testimony that, yes, there was a build-up of violence between Muslims and Serbs, including armed violence from Serb forces? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to say that, but that's what happened then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: And there was a great deal of fear and people were doing guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, was there an arming of Bosnian Muslims in reaction or because of the build-up of violence?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. The truth is that there was a protest when the army arrived and wanted to take away the military booklets, records. They didn't want to give them up. But before that, the army had taken away all the weapons. Everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, you're referring to the army as being the JNA army?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: As a result of the build-up of tension leading to armed conflict, and during the armed conflict during the spring of 1992, did you go to the village of Suceska to stay?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Upon my return from Bratunac, I went home. I had fifty chickens, a month old. I packed them up, put them in my trailer and with Sulja Sedunin [phoen] and Abdurahmanovic I got into my car and drove off towards Suceska. At Viogor five Serb soldiers stopped me with weapons and they carried out a search.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Bogilovic, after being stopped by the Serb soldiers, did you eventually make it to the house of person named Zulfo Tursunovic in Suceska?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: That's two kilometres away. Yes. I found his wife there and I asked her whether I could leave my chickens there, and she said that I could, so I left my chickens there and as that's where his house is and his brother's house, I carried on into the village to look for food with which to feed my chickens.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, did you know Mr. Zulfo Tursunovic prior to May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, how long did you stay in the village or near the village of Suceska in the month of May? Until what date?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: I think that I stayed there a total, in fact until the 22nd, 23rd, 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to turn your attention now to the 20th of May. Mr. Bogilovic, were you in the village of Bajramovici on the 20th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is the village in the municipality of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please explain, briefly explain to the Trial Chamber the reason that you were in the village of Bajramovici on the 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: The reason was because Zulfo had told me, while I was in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. village of Suceska, Zulfo had told me to come to his house. When I got there, to his house, he told me an attack had been carried out and there are killings in Bratunac and in the municipality of Vlasenica. An ultimatum was issued to the village of Bajramovici to move out and to go to Turkey, and that the time has come for us to do something. He said that Ustic Akif would come to Bajramovici and asked me whether I wanted to go to Bajramovici with them and I said that I wanted to go there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: About how many persons were present in the village of Bajramovici when you went there?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: When we got there in the village, the entire village attended the rally, all the inhabitants. There were several young men from Potocari who had come from Potocari, and Akif had come.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you tell the Trial Chamber whether there were about under 100 or over 100 persons present at this time.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: I think that nobody counted them. I didn't count them, but the entire village was there, it must have been thereabouts. Plus, minus, that would be the figure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was a person that you knew of named Naser Oric present at this gathering in Bajramovici?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Had you known this person named Naser Oric before this meeting or gathering in Bajramovici?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had known him from when he came to work for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Does that mean that you knew him when he came to work while you were a police officer?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was Mr. Naser Oric also a police officer?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a police officer. I had information that he was in the special units in Belgrade, with Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Does that mean that Mr. Naser Oric followed schooling similar to yours prior to being named a police officer?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Most probably, yes. He should have graduated from the police school, but as for any other specialist training, there were special courses, training for that, seminars.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Naser Oric, in addition to studying at any police school before becoming a police officer, also took special courses or special training in order to become a guard with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I hate to object. He didn't say guard with Milosevic, he talked about special --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- special units in Belgrade with Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct. Could you rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, I stand corrected. Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Naser Oric therefore had any additional training in order to become part of a special unit in Belgrade, in addition to the training at the police school?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I could not vouch for that because that's not something that I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, you testified that there was a person named Akif Ustic who was present. Did you know Mr. Akif Ustic prior to this meeting or this gathering in Bajramovici?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And what context did you know Mr. Ustic prior to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: He was a teacher, of physical education.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you know whether there was a person named Hamdija Fejzic present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Hamdija Fejzic was present at the meeting. He was a resident of the village of Bajramovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was there a person named Ahmo Tihic present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Ahmo Tihic prior to the meeting in Bajramovici?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did know him. He was a driver. He worked at the transport company in Bajina Basta in Serbia, and then later on he had his own company for transportation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Trial Chamber what, if anything, resulted from the gathering in Bajramovici on the 20th of May with the persons that you have just told us who were present.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: The biggest reason was the fear, the fear of the people and an appeal launched by the people to do something, for people to come together to prevent what had happened in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, what did happen then, as a result of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: That was mostly because of the fear, because there were mass arrests in Bratunac and in Vlasenica, and people wanted to come together to gather and to set up guards. That was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And what type of guards or what types of setting up or any type of designations were made at the meeting in Bajramovici, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: If any attack should happen on the other villages, then all the other villages would help the village under the attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: That was how it was set up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, at the meeting in Bajramovici, were you asked to do any special task?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: I was not asked to do anything. The only thing was that Akif Ustic said that Srebrenica had been devastated and plundered, that there was a threat of an epidemic and that refugees had become to come in and that I should go to Srebrenica to set up law and order, to set up a police station there so that law and order could be re-established.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you accept the responsibility that was asked to set up a police station at that meeting in Bajramovici?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was the person you described as Naser Oric, was he asked to assume any responsibility that day at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but assignments were handed out at that time and this is what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: What assignments were handed out at that time in relationship to the person described as Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was supposed to be the commander of the staff, the staff for salvation. It seemed to me more like a staff that was tasked with saving the town. This was the name that they used for some reason, and this name just stuck, the staff, the term. Akif was supposed to be his deputy and Hamdija was to still remain in Bajramovici, another person in Suceska, and Josic [phoen] was to remain in his village where he had been before, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was there any special responsibility or task given to the person you described as Zulfo Tursunovic?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody in fact was given any special task. The only person to get a special task was myself. I was told to call up all the police officers that used to be police officers before and to set up this police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, do you recall whether the staff of the Srebrenica TO was formed on that day in Bajramovici?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: I remember 20th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And do you remember whether the territorial staff of the Srebrenica municipality was formed on that day, or not?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: This is when we called it the staff. We, who were there. In fact, the people delegated to Zulfo, the village of Potocari delegated Naser, Srebrenica delegated Akif, Bajramovici Hamdija, and the only thing was that I was tasked by them to be the police officers in charge of police.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, did Mr. Oric on that occasion accept to be the commander designated by Potocari of the territorial staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The witness hasn't accepted it was the territorial staff. He talked about first of all the staff of salvation, then he said we call it the staff. He hasn't accepted it was a territorial staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact that is the first time that I am hearing the term "territorial staff," and that is by you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I asked that in a prior question. If you just give me one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your question was, "And do you remember whether the territorial staff of Srebrenica municipality was formed on that day?" And he had answered, "This is when we called it the staff, who we -- we who were there." But he didn't say it was territorial staff, he said that they called it a staff, so let's keep calling it a staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, let me just rephrase that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Srebrenica staff, basically. I mean, because it's more or less... That's the impression I got from his answers, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Then to your knowledge, did Mr. Oric, on that occasion, accept to be the commander designated by Potocari of the Srebrenica staff?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: There were two proposals. One was for Mr. Oric and the other one was for Mr. Ustic. And there was a vote and the result was that Mr. Oric be appointed the commander and Mr. Akif Ustic was to be his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And who participated in the voting?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: We did. The people that was present there. In fact, not all could fit into this room, because it was not a large room.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And as a result of that voting, is it your testimony that Mr. Oric then accepted to be the commander of the Srebrenica staff?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We all accepted. Oric accepted to be the commander, Mr. Ustic to be his commander, Zulfo accepted to go back to Suceska, Hamdija to Bajramovici, and I accepted to go back to Srebrenica to establish a police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: During that meeting you mentioned that there was a person called Hamdija Fejzic present. Would you please tell the Trial Chamber what, if anything, he was doing during the meeting.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Hamdija took the minutes. He had a notebook and a pencil and he was taking notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, you mentioned that Akif Ustic, or Ustic, accepted to be -- on the transcript it says "to be his commander." Was Akif Ustic -- accepted Naser Oric to be his commander, or did you want to say something different?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: No. In fact, it was decided and accepted that Naser be the commander, and that Mr. Ustic be his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like Mr. Bogilovic to be shown P73. Mr. Bogilovic will be shown the original. I believe that we have copies. Could I please have the usher assist us with the original here that we will give to the witness. I've been informed that the English translation, in particular the second page of the English translation, is not in Sanction, so I would ask you to, when I refer to that second page, please refer to your copy on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have it here. We have the second page. So if necessary, we will put the second page on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, I would ask you to look at the document before you.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: I did see this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to draw your attention to the last paragraph of the document, that's entitled: Statement of reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It's on the second page of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, I would like to ask you: Are these some of the reasons that the meeting in Bajramovici was called on the 20th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: The main reason was the attacks of the Serbian units and the arrests of the various persons and the fear.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was there also a need that was seen by the people who had gathered in Bajramovici that day, to self-organise and to merge self-organised groups into larger units?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was there also expressed by people that day, and a result of the meeting, the creation of a single military command of all the armed groups within the Srebrenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly. The problem was because of the relief, because we could not establish links between our units because there were Serb units between us and if we want to send our couriers to establish communication with other units, many of our couriers never came back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, I would now like to ask you to turn your attention to section 2 of this document. Does section 2 of this document accurately reflect your testimony of the appointments of Naser Oric as commander and that of Akif Ustic as deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: This is correct. This is how it was, and for the first time, in this format, and this is the -- I saw this paper for the first time when Mr. Nasir showed it to me and it was recorded in a notebook in pencil.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: May I just correct for the record that the Nasir that I believe that Mr. Bogilovic at this point is speaking about is the investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor. I do not want to mislead anyone on that. Mr. Bogilovic, the first time you saw this was handwritten? Is that what your testimony is, in terms of your first visual looking of a document that had that information on it?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Which? There are two here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm talking about the document that is before you. You just testified that the first time you saw it was in handwriting.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: I saw this document for the first time when Mr. Nasir showed it to me in Austria.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: May I draw your attention further down to number 6, where it says "Becir Bogilovic from Srebrenica is a member of the Srebrenica TO staff, an outstanding activist in armed resistance against the aggressor in the area of Suceska." Is that a reference to you, Mr. Bogilovic?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is precise reference to me, because the practice was, at all times in the previous system, if you want to appoint somebody for -- to some post, you have to write some good things about him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And is that why they wrote that you were "an outstanding activist in armed resistance against the aggressor"?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Probably, yes, because I was a policeman as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, will you also just confirm, then, that the mentioning of Hamdija Fejzic, Sefkic Jokic [phoen], and also Ahmo Tihic conformed to what you witnessed that day in Bajramovici in terms of the appointments to the Srebrenica staff?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: As far as Hamdija is concerned -- yes, Hamdija, because he was in front of the people, Bajramovici; Zulfo was the Suceska people; Jusofovic was from Srebrenica; and Oric Naser was from Potocari, representing them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please turn to or look at the bottom of that document, where you see the name Hamdija Fejzic written. Do you recall that day that Hamdija Fejzic was taking notes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has already said it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I will withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you: Prior to you being shown this document by the investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor, had you seen the signature of a person called Naser Oric on any occasion?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: The first time I saw it was when we had this meeting and when I was given the task of setting up a police station. Then they were supposed to give me two members, two people. And the people they were sending, they had to write down their names. So that was the first time that I saw that Zulfo sent me two people, Oric sent me two people, and the third man sent me two people, and that was in 1992. And I saw this because in 1995, on the 18th of April, on paper, appointing me, that's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Can I clarify, so that I understand correctly, are you stating that you'd seen the signature of a person called Naser Oric on two occasions because you were sent -- people were sent to you from him?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you also see the signature of Naser Oric, prior to the investigator from the OTP showing you this document on a third occasion?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: In 1995 -- no, 1993 on the 18th of April, 1993. And I never saw it up until I was shown it by Mr. Nasir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like you to look at the signature on the bottom, left-hand side of the document before you. And could you recognise that as a signature of a person of the Naser Oric who was present at the meeting in Bajramovici?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: This is a signature in Cyrillic, in the Cyrillic script. I used to write in Cyrillic 45 years ago but never since then. Now, Oric --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, I would like you to -- for the sake of our time period here, to respond to the question of whether you recognise the signature on the bottom, left-hand side of this document as a signature of the Naser Oric who was present at the meeting in Bajramovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Left-hand --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Left-hand, yes. I'm left handed so I get that confused. So bottom, left-hand corner of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we see the original, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, right-hand corner of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right-hand side. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have a case of dyslexia here. Let's put it on the ELMO, please. Okay. Let's try and follow. Yes. We are referring you to the signature which is partly hidden by the stamp, on the bottom right. Do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say 100 percent. It is similar, but I'm not an expert myself, so I can't say 100 percent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the one on the left, do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never saw that until I was shown it by Mr. Nasir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, you say you can't be 100 per cent sure, but does that signature resemble a signature that you have seen before by a person called Naser Oric who was present at the meeting in Bajramovici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even if he tells you yes, Ms. Sellers, you wouldn't have advanced one inch.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can only repeat what I said. When you read the letters, it says Oric, but I can't guarantee who signed it, when they signed it, because I didn't see the document. And when we made this decision, nobody signed anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Does that resemble the signature of Mr. Oric to you, Mr. Bogilovic?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: All the letters that you have in the name Oric are there. There's the O, there's the R, there's the I there's the C diacritic. Now who wrote it, whether he wrote it or someone else, I would leave that up to the experts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, did you speak with the Office of the Prosecutor, investigator Naser Oric and -- I'm sorry. D. A. Nasir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "Mr. Nasir."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Nasir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: On the 7th of December in 2003?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 7th of December.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the date was, but I did talk to him when he came to Austria.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is that when Mr. Nasir first showed you this document?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: I saw that document for the first time then, in this particular format.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And do you recall what you said to Mr. Nasir when he enquired as to the signature in the bottom, right-hand corner of the document?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, most probably I said that it was similar to Oric. It resembled Oric, but that I couldn't confirm whether it was indeed his signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And is that your testimony today, Mr. Bogilovic?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course. That's what I'm saying -- stating.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bogilovic.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: But it's a matter for the experts. You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to have the document removed from the witness now. I would like to have the witness shown P74. The original will be shown to the witness and I think everyone else has their copy. The English version is placed in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, would you please look at the document before you.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: I've seen it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Could you confirm that this document reflects the responsibilities that you were given to organise the police force at that meeting in Bajramovici on the 20th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Since I saw this document for the first time, or rather, when I saw it -- I assume that when I was appointed this is the way it was written for me to react, because it says "We appoint Becir Bogilovic as a policeman, from Srebrenica, a policeman, the former commander of Srebrenica SJB is appointed temporary police commander in the town of Srebrenica." I know that the decision was made then for me to be the komandir, commander, and to equip the police in Srebrenica, and no kind of deputy, temporary anything or --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Pardon me. Mr. Bogilovic, I would like to draw your attention to section 1 of the document where it says that you were a former commander of Srebrenica SJB. Now, is that also a way of puffery to make the person feel better or were you actually a former commander of the Srebrenica SJB?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: In the notebook that Hamdija wrote in, according to Akif's proposals, it should have said: As a komandir, commander, and not in the way this was written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You haven't answered the question. Before you were given this special assignment, to go back to Srebrenica and organise this, all of this, you had been employed in the Srebrenica public security station, no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was a pensioner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But before you became a pensioner, you had been a policeman stationed in Srebrenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's right, in September 1991, as the sector leader, and that's how I retired. I retired as a sector leader.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So when they say here, in this document, "Becir Bogilovic from Srebrenica, a policeman, the former commander of Srebrenica SJB," is that what they are referring to, that you were the sector -- sector leader in Srebrenica? Or is it your position your previous position is being inflated to appear as if you had been the commander of the Srebrenica public security station? This is the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Yes. I've understood what you said. I think that this has been puffed up, because there's a lot of difference here, this notion of komandir and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Leader or whatever is not the commander of the SJB. Go ahead, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, I would also draw your attention to section 2, toward the end of the paragraph, the large paragraph, where it states that you're temporarily accountable. "He shall be temporarily accountable for his work to the Srebrenica TO staff, to the above bodies once they have been set up and to the authorised institutions in Tuzla and Sarajevo when they too have been set up." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what this meant to you or means to you in the document.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: This list probably meant that because they appointed me. So it would be normal for me to be responsible to them because there were no other institutions or levels in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In your understanding, were you appointed to be the civilian police chief?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: I was appointed commandeer of the civilian police on the 20th of May, 1992. For the chief of police, I was appointed on the 1st of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you come under the authorities that were civilian authorities in Srebrenica when you were appointed in July, on the 1st of July?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of July, that was when the decision was taken to set up a wartime Presidency, and I was subordinated to the wartime Presidency and President Avdic Hajrudin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If I could ask that the document now be taken from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sellers. And thank you, usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, in addition to the appointments that you have just testified that took place as a result of the meeting on the 20th of May in Bajramovici, were there other people in the month of May, 1992 that were appointed to the Srebrenica staff?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: The people that we talked about on the 20th of May, 1992, in view of the situation -- well, actually, just one part. Suceska, Bajram, Potocari, and Srebrenica were included there. So for this area to expand and include other villages, what was done was that the organisation was expanded.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Atif Krdzic?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. I know him well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber who is he or particularly who he was in that time period in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, Akif Krdzic --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: -- was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Krdzic, Krestic [phoen]. Please excuse my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Ah, you mean -- could you please try and pronounce the names better, because there is Akif Hrustic and Akif Krdzic, so which person are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm referring to the person whose name begins with a K.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you have difficulties, you can confidently rely on either Mr. Wubben or -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In the future I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure you will find all the comfort that you need, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Krdzic, Kresdzic [phoen]. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm referring to him, Mr. Bogilovic. Could you please continue and explain to the Trial Chamber who he was or position he had in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: In May 1992, Atif Krdzic, he was born in the village of Osmace in the municipality of Srebrenica. He was a police officer in the public security station. And when I came to Srebrenica to establish the police station there, I was authorised to call up all the active serving police officers that I could reach, and I sent a courier to him. But the people said, He cannot go. He must stay here, because the people are still afraid. And since the people trusted the police, they wanted him to stay there, and that is why he remained there in his own village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, did he become a member of the Srebrenica staff in May 1992, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: As the staff expanded, all those who were appointed by the people automatically became members of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did that include Mr. Atif Krdzic?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Most likely, yes. Because the people made the choice.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, in regard to Nedzad Bektic. Did he become a member of the Srebrenica staff in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Also.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would also like to ask you in regard to Senahid Tabahric. Did he become a member of the Srebrenica staff in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would the witness please be handed document P75. The original will be shown to the witness. I believe we have the others. It's also in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, will you please look at the document in front of you, and could you please confirm for the Trial Chamber that it reflects your testimony, particularly in relationship to Mr. Bektic and Mr. Tabahric, that the Srebrenica staff expanded in the month of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: I can confirm that the staff expanded and that this was written in pencil in a notebook. And I have to apologise for repeating this every time. The first time that I saw this, in this form, was when Mr. Nasir showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And is the first person on that list, beside number 1, was that person also a part of the Srebrenica staff as of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Atif Krdzic, is that who you mean? Of course, yes. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And do you recognize the name on the bottom left-hand corner of the document?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: It says Hamdija Fejzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And do you recognise the signature of the person on the right-hand corner of the document as that of Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: I can say the same thing as I had already said, because I was not there when the document was signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bogilovic.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We can please take the document from him at this point in time. Your Honour, did you want to make an announcement at this time period or should I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. We will continue until 4.00, since we started at half past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we will have 25 -- 20 or 25-minute break. And then we will continue till 6.00 or thereabouts. Or maybe five minutes beyond that. But not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, right now I would like to talk about the organisation of the civilian police. In the month of May 1992, would you explain to the Trial Chamber as succinctly as possible how you took upon your task to organise the civilian police in the municipality of Srebrenica. Mr. Bogilovic, might I ask you, would you please tell the Trial Chamber and Defence counsel as well as the Prosecution what you are reading from?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: This is -- these are the notes that I took, kind of a diary. If this is not allowed, I cannot make use of that. It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What kind of a diary? When did you write those notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wrote that now, in the recent days, because in the statement that I gave here during -- as I was giving the statement, I was making these notes in order to make it easier for me to remember some details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you think you will need those notes in order to refresh your memory from time to time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I think. But I -- I can put them aside. Whatever you decide, I, of course, will abide by your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you are going to -- if we are going to allow you to make use of those notes, I need to make it clear to you that you need also to make them available to us. In other words, we will have a copy of them and they will be made available to the Prosecution and to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, yes, if you want, you can have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the witness is going to be using his notes, I would like to have copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers, have you seen those notes already? Or not yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I have not seen those notes in order to read them. I notice that during the sessions of proofing at times Mr. Bogilovic would be writing, at other times he would be doodling on paper. So I do not know whether this might be a combination of both. I would suggest that he answer questions without the notes. If he needs, in any way, to have his memory refreshed, that might be a different issue. But I would suggest that we begin without the notes. They're not anything I wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, if you are going to make use of those notes, then obviously we need to see them. All right. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, did you begin to organise, in May 1992, the civilian police force in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: When I was appointed on the 20th of May, 1992, since all my staff was in Suceska and also my chickens, I went there to Suceska to get all that stuff, and then three or four days later I returned to Srebrenica. Since my house had been burned, I went to see a colleague of mine. We had worked together for 20 years, and I asked him if I could live in his place and he said, of course. So that's where I stayed, at his place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, excuse me, very briefly would you explain to the Trial Chamber how your house was burned, or when and how your house was burned.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date. It must have been around the 4th of May. It wasn't just my house. 88 houses in total had been burnt.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And were those houses burned as a result of armed Serb forces or armed Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: My house and all the other houses, when the Serb units went in, the Serbian company that got in on the 18th of April, 1992, it was commanded by Pero nicknamed Zimunitz [phoen]. That was a whole company of this military, and they also had some local Serbs with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And were they the --

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: And they started committing crimes of plundering houses, taking various electronic goods, and arresting people. They burned 88 houses, killed seven whole families. Killed a family of young people, including their three children. They killed a disabled person, a retired police officer who was unable to walk, Abdurahmanovic was also killed in the police station, the headmaster, and when I got to the police station, in view of the situation, these people had been killed, the station was torn down, and I did not agree to go and to work there in this police station building.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay, excuse me, Mr. Bogilovic.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: So I went --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, can I just clarify. Your house was burned down as a result of Serb army in April, is that what you've just told the Trial Chamber? Yes?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Could we --

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Not in April. In May.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In May.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: In May. The 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could we return to your explaining to the Trial Chamber how you set up the civilian police force also in May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: How did you gather the men who had come within the civilian police force?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akif Ustic, said when he proposed me, he said that this should be done as soon as possible because there was a risk of an epidemic, refrigerators didn't work, food was rotting, there was no water supply, and the refugees from the area of Bratunac started coming to Srebrenica and that was the reason why law and order should be re-established as soon as possible. He said that he had appointed some police officers but he was not happy with them. When I got there, when I learned about any active duty police officers, I called them up, since there were very few of them. Then Naser sent me two, Hamdija sent me two people, Zulfo sent me two people, and I was able to establish the police force in the building of the territorial defence staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bogilovic. When you say that Naser sent you two, Zulfo sent you two, are you referring to Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Naser Oric. Because it was agreed at that time that all of them should send me two people each.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And is that the same Naser Oric that was with you on the 20th of May in Bajramovici?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's the same person. There is no other.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When the two officers or the two persons sent you by Naser Oric, did he send any paperwork with those two persons?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: I think I did say a little while ago he did send something, because they needed to have a sheet telling them to report to me. It was just a piece of paper and it was handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And what did the piece of paper say, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Full name of that person and his signature and the instructions to report to me. It said I am sending you these two persons to be police officers, and that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Whose signature was on the documents?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Oric's.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When you say "Oric," or you say "Naser," can I assume that you're always referring to Naser Oric who was at the meeting on the 20th in Bajramovici?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm always referring to him because there was no other person. There was only this one man.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you stated that Zulfo and other persons who were on the Srebrenica staff also sent you persons to man your civilian police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you have a deputy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because there is something in the transcript that I -- I want to make sure that it will not be misinterpreted at any time. The witness is reported as having answered, "I'm always referring to him because there was no other person. There was only this one man." Basically, what you are telling us is that there was only one Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, did you have a deputy to assist you in the forming and the functioning of the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: When Nedzad Bektic became part of the staff, he proposed a man by the name of Nurija, who used to be a police officer, that this person be made my deputy. And this was accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber, what was the family name, last name, the surname of Nurija.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Nurija Jusofovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Trial Chamber where, if anywhere, the offices of the civilian police were located in the month of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: In May 1992, we were in the Territorial Defence Staff building. We took over their offices.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like the witness to look at the monitor for Sanction, and also the Trial Chamber. There is a picture, the ER -- I have to be advised of the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: I can see this photograph. This building is the Territorial Defence Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, indicating the building that is of to the left-hand side of the screen that appears to be yellow, or are you indicating a building that is to the right-hand side of the screen that appears to be quite dark?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: No. This one right in the middle. The building to the left is the skyscraper, the whiter one; and this one that appears to be dirty, this is the one that was partially burned down when fire was set to it. This was due to smoke. But this is an integral part of this building.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We will place one on the ELMO so that the witness will be able to also indicate. Mr. Bogilovic, would you look at the picture on the ELMO and, please, could you point to where the offices of the civilian police were located.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would ask that the picture be moved down.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters apologise, we did not hear the witness because he was not speaking into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you point to the building again, Mr. Bogilovic, please, without hiding it with your hand. So for the record, the photograph that the witness is being referred to bears ERN number 03650237 and the witness has pointed, indeed, to the part of the -- to the building that is exactly in the middle between the high rising building and the other one on the right, which shows -- the signs of burning and which has the words "Lukic" written across. Yes, we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, I would like to ask you, that part of the building that you are pointing to that appears to be lighter, is that joined to the upper part of the building that appears to be darker? Is that a building that is joined?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: This is one building. This is all one building. The lighter one and the darker one, that's one and the same building. Because this is where the offices are and this is where the depot of the Territorial Defence Staff was, this area here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Can I have two last questions, Your Honour. Mr. Bogilovic, if you would move your marker down on the dark area of the building, toward the ground, would you explain to the Trial Chamber, what building is that, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: This is the Red Cross building and the building where the sports equipment was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was that a storage facility, to your knowledge, prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: It was the Red Cross and the sports equipment. Bataju Vukisavljevic had it. He was a coach.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did that building have bars on the window, prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did that building have bars on the window during the war, between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody took the bars off.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions on this section. I would ask that the document be taken away from the witness and ask for a P number for it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I think we have seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a photo. What we have seen before is part of a video film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document will become document P516. I thank you. We will have a 20-minute break, if that is agreeable to, first of all, the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then the technicians -- this will be the only break that we will have, but then we will finish at 6.00. I see nodding. Yes. Technicians? I can't see behind the glass.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. We will resume in 20, 25 minutes time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's continue, Ms. Sellers. We are going -- proceeding very, very slowly. It is not your fault, of course. It's someone else's fault, but let's try to finish with this witness today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would say I would try to speak faster but then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I don't think that will help. And you, Mr. Bogilovic, please try to keep your answers as concise, as short and as to-the-point as possible, because I am trying to be able to make sure to send you back home first thing early next week, but at this rate, you are going to be here a long, long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, you were explaining to us where the police offices of the civilian police. I would just like to ask you a couple of questions. Did you have at your disposal a typewriter?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, in the first days, I did not. But I took it from a citizen who happened to find it somewhere. I confiscated it and took it for myself. It wasn't in very good order, some letters were missing, and I would add those letters in pencil, the missing letters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were you also able to get paper to use in the typewriter?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: It was difficult to come by the paper. So we would use any old pieces of paper that we would find. We would have a piece of paper and when we finished writing on one side, we would use the other side, and so made double use of the paper we had available.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just a very small thing, he did say "vilitesko" [phoen] "very difficult." I think it was interpreted as "difficult." It's a small matter, but I think it should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You heard what Mr. Jones said. You agree with that, that you said "very difficult"? Do you agree that you'd said "very difficult" and not just "difficult" to find paper, to procure paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very difficult, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, would you explain to the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- very briefly, what was the function of the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC
utterances.text: The civilian police worked pursuant to the rules of service for the public security service, and as I had worked as an active duty policeman for 20 years, I continued that practice when I was appointed to that post. It is true that I worked as sector leader but I just changed the name. I was komandir.
